items.title: CREST CTF 2.0

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I changed my saved display name, then triggered its use in /colleagues; that exposed a second-order SQL injection.

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I tested the query with ORDER BY and learned it returned two columns. An error confirmed that the application used SQLite.

I used SQLite's json_extract() errors to reveal the table names, the secrets columns (id, name, value), and the secret value.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I found the exposed backup configuration and used its Flask signing key to access the admin report.

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I checked /robots.txt, found /static/backup/, then requested the backup configuration directly because the directory listing returned 404:

curl http://<challenge-host>/static/backup/config.py.bak

I found the Flask SECRET_KEY in the file. I inspected the session cookie, changed its role, signed it with the leaked key, then refreshed /dashboard to open the report.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I found the challenge metadata in the standard security contact file.

items.title: Solve
items.text: I opened /.well-known/security.txt and read the requested value from its metadata.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I revealed the information hidden in the nearly white image at /q.png.

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I downloaded the image and compared its RGB values. I found hidden pixels at (255, 255, 254), one blue-channel value below white. I rendered each non-white pixel black:

curl -s http://<challenge-host>/q.png -o q.png

from PIL import Image

image = Image.open("q.png").convert("RGB")
pixels = image.load()

for y in range(image.height):
    for x in range(image.width):
        if pixels[x, y] != (255, 255, 255):
            pixels[x, y] = (0, 0, 0)

image.save("revealed.png")

The resulting image showed P.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I extracted RSA private-key material from the image metadata and decrypted the provided ciphertext. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I ran exiftool and found hex-encoded key material in the comment:

exiftool image.jpeg

The repeated 2d bytes decode to PEM hyphens. I saved the comment's hex as key.hex, reconstructed the key, then decrypted the file:

xxd -r -p key.hex > rsa_private_key.pem
openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey rsa_private_key.pem -in flag.enc -out decrypt_file.txt

items.title: Challenge
items.text: The challenge lets ctf-player run Nano with sudo. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I opened /etc/sudoers in Nano, added an all-privileges rule for ctf-player, then read the flag:

sudo /bin/nano /etc/sudoers
sudo cat flag.txt

I added this rule: ctf-player ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: The service sends 20 ELF rounds, gives 10 seconds per round, and expects the secret as a decimal number. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I inspected a round's disassembly and found the 32-bit secret in a mov immediate. I read its four little-endian bytes after c7 45 fc and converted them to an unsigned decimal integer.

I used this local extraction for each supplied hex dump:

import re

elf = bytes.fromhex(open("round.hex").read())
match = re.search(rb"\xc7\x45\xfc(.{4})", elf, re.DOTALL)
if match is None:
    raise ValueError("secret immediate not found")
print(int.from_bytes(match.group(1), "little"))

Submit the printed decimal value and repeat for each round.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: The challenge provides ASCII 0 and 1 characters; I packed each group of eight bits into a byte to recover the image. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I inspected the input, packed the bits into bytes, then opened the JPEG:

xxd digits.bin | head -n 10

from pathlib import Path

bits = Path("digits.bin").read_text().split()
bits = "".join(bits)
image = bytes(int(bits[i:i + 8], 2) for i in range(0, len(bits) - 7, 8))
Path("output.jpg").write_bytes(image)

The output starts with a JPEG/JFIF signature. I opened output.jpg and read the flag.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I inspected the local binary's password check to recover the value it compares against. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I used LLDB to inspect the decoded password buffer. The program XORs the stored bytes with 0xaa; the buffer contained SuperSecure at the comparison:

(lldb) expr (char*)($rbp - 0x110)

I entered this password:

SuperSecure

items.title: Solve

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I analyzed a 64-bit program whose oversized input can redirect execution to win. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I checked the local binary and its protections:

file vuln
checksec --file=vuln

The source reads up to 128 bytes into a 32-byte buffer, and checksec showed NX enabled with PIE disabled. I used cyclic input in the debugger to find the return offset, then redirected execution to win and got the flag.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I investigated how a global rate limit interacts with HAProxy's primary/backup health checks and failover. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text: I wrote a script to trigger the HAProxy failover and check the backup response. The backup server returned the flag.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: The portal hides each profile ID behind an MD5 hash. I used the predictable IDs to reach the admin profile. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text: I found the guest login in the page source and signed in. The profile showed ID 3000, and its URL matched the MD5 hash of that number. I used the same pattern to locate the admin profile and read its flag.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: The binary multiplies each flag character by the answer to its arithmetic question, then prints the products. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I inspected the encoding loop in Ghidra. The challenge answer was 36, so I divided each printed value by 36 to recover its character:

values = [
    3492, 3564, 3492, 3600, 3636, 3924, 4356, 4428, 3924, 1872,
    4176, 3744, 3420, 3528, 1836, 3744, 1764, 3960, 3600, 3420,
    3564, 1764, 4032, 3744, 1836, 4104, 3420, 3636, 1800, 3492,
    3564, 3564, 3636, 3528, 3564, 4500,
]
print("".join(chr(value // 36) for value in values))

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I decoded the message's Base64, hex, URL-escaped braces, and ROT13 layers. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I reversed the transformations in order:

base64 -d message_multicode.txt > stage1.hex
xxd -r -p stage1.hex > stage2.txt
cat stage2.txt

The hex-decoded text was npnqrzl%7Barfgrq_rap0qvat_74ns0p65%7D. I replaced the escaped braces and applied ROT13:

sed 's/%7B/{/g; s/%7D/}/g' stage2.txt | rot13

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I pushed a commit with the required author metadata and a flag.txt file. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I set the commit identity, created flag.txt, and pushed the commit:

git config user.name 'root'
git config user.email 'root@picoctf'
touch flag.txt
git add .
git commit -m 'changes'
git push origin master

The server checked the commit author and returned the flag from its push hook.

items.text: I traced the application's second-factor login flow and found the OTP in its session data. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text: I found the admin's SHA-256 password hash in users.db, recovered the password offline with the supplied wordlist, and logged in. I decoded the Flask session and read the OTP there; I didn't need to brute-force it.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I used CUPP to generate a wordlist from the supplied personal details, then ran it through the provided password checker. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I cloned CUPP and ran its interactive profile mode:

git clone https://github.com/Mebus/cupp.git
cd cupp
python3 cupp.py -i

I put the generated list in the challenge directory and ran the checker:

python3 check_password.py

The checker found the password, and I used it to get the flag.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I concatenated the five archive fragments, entered the password, and read the flag. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I concatenated the parts in order, ran unzip, entered supersecret, and read flag.txt:

cat part_aa > part.zip
cat part_ab >> part.zip
cat part_ac >> part.zip
cat part_ad >> part.zip
cat part_ae >> part.zip
unzip part.zip
cat flag.txt

items.title: Challenge

items.text:
I listed the shares anonymously, connected to shares, and downloaded the flag:

smbclient -L //<challenge-host> -p <challenge-port> -N
smbclient //<challenge-host>/shares -p <challenge-port> -N
smb: \> get flag.txt

items.title: Challenge
items.text: The secret-creation endpoint interpolates user content directly into an SQL statement.

items.title: Solve
items.text: I traced /secrets/create and found that it inserted content directly into the query. I used that injection to copy the admin's secret into my own account, then read the flag from my secrets list.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I reversed the local password database binary and inspected the value its hash routine returned. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
The program XORs the hidden input bytes with 0xaa, then applies a 64-bit DJB2-style hash. I set a breakpoint on hash, ran the program, and inspected its return value:

(gdb) break hash
(gdb) run
(gdb) finish
(gdb) info registers rax

GDB returned the signed value -3209081493549540382.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I computed the shared value from the supplied Diffie–Hellman parameters and used it to decode the ciphertext. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
The challenge leaked the private exponent b. I plugged its A, b, p, and hex ciphertext into this code:

shared = pow(A, b, p)
key_byte = shared & 0xff
ciphertext = bytes.fromhex(enc)
plaintext = bytes(byte ^ key_byte for byte in ciphertext)
print(plaintext)

I checked my sudo permissions, launched Emacs with sudo, used M-x shell, and read flag.txt:

items.title: Challenge
items.text: I reversed the sequence of text transformations to recover the flag. Challenge page

items.title: Solve
items.text:
I decoded the Base64, reversed the text, restored underscores and braces, then applied ROT13:

base64 -d | rev | tr '-' '_' | tr '()' '{}' | tr 'a-zA-Z' 'n-za-mN-ZA-M'
